newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: King condemns any Khmer Rouge link, outside help.
newsitem.headline: King condemns any Khmer Rouge link, outside help.

text.p: Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk on Monday condemned any alliance with Khmer Rouge guerrilla factions and called on foreign powers not to help either side in his country's latest conflict.
Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousted Sihanouk's son, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh on July 6 after two days of fighting in the capital.
Hun Sen's troops have been fighting forces loyal to Ranariddh and some Khmer Rouge guerrillas in northern Cambodia since the prince's ouster.
"I absolutely condemn all alliances with the Khmer Rouge," from whatever guerrilla faction, he said in an interview with his bulletin.
A transcript of the interview was released in Beijing where Sihanouk is having medical treatment.
The Khmer Rouge, responsible for the death of more than a million Cambodians during their 1975-79 rule, has recently split into several factions.

"These Khmer Rouge have committed unforgivable crimes against humanity. It is very immoral to use them in this very ugly struggle for power which has cost so much loss, ruin, misery suffering and despair to our innocent little people," he said.
Ranariddh announced in May that he had opened negotiations with the Khmer Rouge in an effort to end their war against the government.

The prince also said he would be willing to form a political alliance with the group's main political leader, Khieu Samphan, if he announced he had broken with supreme leader Pol Pot and recognised the Cambodian constitution.
The king said that Ranariddh's forces had been "smashed" in the recent fighting with the "very superior" forces under Hun Sen.

The king was asked if he thought Vietnam had helped Hun Sen in his ouster of Ranariddh and responded by saying he did not have an intelligence service like the French or the United States to determine the true situation but he appealed to countries not to assist either side in the conflict.

"I have to ask all foreign countries, without exception, not to give any help, whatever the nature of this help, to belligerent Cambodians awfully engaged in the abominable, unjustifiable enterprise of destruction between Cambodians," he said.

Hun Sen justified his forces' move against Ranariddh's men in the capital by saying Ranariddh's military commanders were smuggling defectors from the Khmer Rouge into the city to bolster the prince's troops strength. Ranariddh denied he was doing so.
Vietnam has denied giving any assistance to Hun Sen who was in Vietnam on July 5, the day his forces moved against Ranariddh's men in the capital. Hanoi said he was on a private visit.
